p.x:
Look at this poster! It's an advert for a new ice cream. The colours are bright, and there's a nice picture of a smiling girl at the beach. The words say, "The best ice cream in the world!"
My little brother saw the poster and said, "I want that ice cream!" My mum laughed. "Is it really the best?" she asked. "Adverts always say that."
We bought one to try. It was good, but it wasn't the best. My mum says adverts want you to buy things, so they make everything look perfect. The beach in the picture isn't real, either. It was made on a computer! Now, when I see an advert, I ask myself: is this true?

Every day, we see hundreds of adverts: on TV, on billboards, on buses and on our phones. Companies spend billions of baht on marketing because adverts are very effective at persuading people to buy things.
Advertisers use many tricks. Some adverts have a catchy jingle that you can't stop singing. Others show popular celebrities who endorse the product. Some offer a free gift, or say that a product is a limited edition, so you feel you must buy it quickly.
Adverts also try to give a product a special image. A car advert might show a happy family in the mountains, while a perfume advert might show a beautiful couple in Paris. The message is: buy this, and your life will be like this.
However, some adverts are misleading. They exaggerate or make claims that aren't true. In Thailand and many other countries, there are rules to stop this. If a company promises a guarantee, it must give one. Next time you watch TV, notice how adverts in the commercial break try to attract and convince you. What makes them unique, and do they really promote what they say?

Advertising has always been about persuasion, but the methods have changed dramatically. In the twentieth century, a single television advert could reach millions of viewers at once. Today, adverts are ubiquitous: we are bombarded with them on social media, in apps, in games and even inside the films we watch, through product placement.
Modern advertisers rely heavily on data. By tracking our online behaviour, they can show each person adverts tailored to their interests, a practice that is extremely effective but raises serious privacy concerns. Psychologists note that many adverts are designed to manipulate emotions rather than provide information. An advert's appeal may depend less on what the product does than on how it makes us feel: younger, more attractive or more successful.
Critics also point out that advertising can reinforce harmful stereotypes, for example by showing women mainly in the kitchen or by presenting unrealistic body images. Others worry about adverts aimed at children, who may not recognise a gimmick such as a free toy for what it is. For this reason, many countries regulate advertising to children, and some ban adverts for unhealthy food during children's programmes.
The idea of subliminal advertising, hidden messages that influence us without our awareness, has fascinated the public for decades, although its real effects appear limited. More concerning, perhaps, are deceptive practices that are openly visible but rarely questioned. As advertising becomes harder to distinguish from entertainment, experts argue that it deserves greater public scrutiny.
